extracted.intended_audience: educated Victorian readers; cultural critics; middle-class readers interested in politics, social reform, and moral philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: An essayistic rubric for judging social, political, and moral operations (e.g., free-trade policy, marriage-law reform) by cultural and ethical standards — contrasting 'Hellenism' (free play of consciousness, reason, culture) with 'Hebraism' (mechanical literalism, fetish-worship).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hellenise test / intelligible law of things
rubrics_metrics.description: "let the natural stream of our consciousness flow over them freely"; examine how a proposed operation is "related to the intelligible law of human life, and to national well-being and happiness."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Hellenising method: let consciousness play freely on the facts; do not accept mechanical or party-maximizing reasoning. If an operation accords with the intelligible law of things revealed by reflection, it may be endorsed.

rubrics_metrics.name: General perfection / culture embraces all fellow-men
rubrics_metrics.description: "culture...conceive of no perfection as being real which is not a general perfection, embracing all our fellow-men with whom we have to do."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge reforms by whether they advance shared human perfection and solidarity — individual gains that leave others degraded are not true perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: True freedom as service / elevation of the best self
rubrics_metrics.description: "the only perfect freedom is, as our religion says, a service; not a service to any stock maxim, but an elevation of our best self."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies and personal conduct should be measured by their capacity to cultivate the best aspects of human nature (delicacy, sympathy, spiritual and intellectual enlargement), not by mere license for the 'ordinary self.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanical worship of fetishes (production/population/free-trade)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat free-trade, the production of wealth, manufactures, or population growth as "an end in itself" or a "fetish" to be worshipped mechanically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate economic policies by their relation to overall human well-being, not by raw metrics like number of manufactories or population increase. Beware of pursuing such objects 'staunchly and mechanically.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical social consequences (poverty, pauper rates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure policies against concrete social outcomes — e.g., the text notes "about one in nineteen of our population is a pauper."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A policy that increases manufactures or population but also increases or fails to reduce pauperism is suspect; use empirical indicators (poverty rates, living standards) to judge success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of religious texts vs reason (contextual use of scripture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation of Bishop Wilson: "Christian duties are founded on reason, not on the sovereign authority of God commanding what he pleases."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply scripture and religious authority prudently and contextually; do not interpret Biblical law mechanically when reason and the necessities of human nature demand otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delicacy of perception in personal relations (love and marriage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate "delicacy of perception" and the ability "to enter with tact and sympathy into the subtle instinctive propensions and repugnances" of others in matters of love and marriage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate sexual/marital reforms by whether they promote subtle sympathy, tact, and enlargement of spiritual/intellectual life rather than merely permitting private liberty without moral sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness over partisanship
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic insists "we who are not partisans can afford" to be disinterested and to let consciousness float stock habits of thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess reforms independently of party loyalties; policies should be judged on their merits relative to human perfection, not on whether they favor a political faction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject necessitarian fatalism; value speculation and thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposes claims like The Times' "what is wanted is not the light of speculation" and the fatalistic 'result of Nature's simplest laws.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept that social evils are inevitable; deliberate, speculative thought is necessary to understand and remedy social problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate possessions/children by relation to progress toward perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: The possession and multiplication of children (or horses, pictures) "is to be accounted good or bad...with reference to this object [progress towards perfection]."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private and familial choices should be judged by whether they aid or hinder personal and communal progress to perfection; having children while unable to support them is morally wrong in this scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural test: give 'commendable interest' only if operation stands the consciousness-test
rubrics_metrics.description: "let us in each case keep testing these operations in the simple way we have indicated, by letting the natural stream of our consciousness flow over them freely; and if they stand this test successfully, then let us give them our commendable interest."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practical approval procedure: only endorse or join a reform after reflective, disinterested testing against the intelligible law of things and the Hellenising standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't treat axioms as self-acting laws without planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of Liberal axioms applied "as if they were self-acting laws which will put themselves into operation without trouble or planning."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using abstract economic or social axioms (e.g., population/production relations), require concrete planning and mechanisms; do not assume automatic beneficial outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of produced goods to subsistence
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: increase of silk-stockings does not relieve scarcity of bread and bacon; production may be unrelated to population needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the kind and distribution of production produced by policy — increased manufactures are valuable only insofar as they improve basic human subsistence and welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual reading of scriptural injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Scriptural texts (e.g., the psalm-verse praising many children) must be read contextually — "composed at the resettlement of Jerusalem after the Captivity" — not applied universally without regard to circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid literalist or ahistorical uses of scripture in policymaking; check whether the scriptural prescription actually fits contemporary social conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture's aim: form minds for fruitful, long-term reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Main business is not crude immediate reforms but to "create, through the help of that culture...a frame of mind out of which really fruitful reforms may with time grow."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize cultural and intellectual cultivation that prepares people for solid, durable reforms rather than immediate partisan action; favor long-term formation of public consciousness.
